newsitem.title: KENYA: Pro-reform Kenya bank governor re-appointed.
newsitem.headline: Pro-reform Kenya bank governor re-appointed.

text.p: Central Bank of Kenya (CBK) Governor Micah Cheserem, a leader of economic reform, was re-appointed for four more years on Thursday in a move that should help calm markets in a turbulent election year.
Mark Lesiit, his personal assistant, said Cheserem was re-appointed by President Daniel arap Moi.
Leading businessmen said they were elated because continuity at the central bank was important and Cheserem's management had proved perhaps the best at CBK since independence in 1963.

"Mr Cheserem is open, prepared to dialogue, interested in listening and putting forward issues," Manu Chandaria, chairman of the Kenya Association of Manufacturers, told Reuters. "He has been the most outstanding governor in post-independence Kenya."
Foreign exchange and equity markets were jolted this month when police violently dispersed demonstrators on July 7 at rallies to press for political reforms before elections.
Lesiit said the re-appointment took effect on Thursday and would be announced in the government gazette on Friday.
Cheserem, 47, took over as governor in July 1993 at the height of financial mismanagement in Kenya's banking system and accusations of corruption at the central bank.
He moved to restore discipline, helping to reduce money supply and cut inflation to current single-digit figures from around 101 percent in October 1993.
Investors had feared Cheserem's term would not be renewed because of his tough approach, which they said would prevent the government from manipulating finances during the 1997 polls.
Charles Gardner, resident representative of the Eastern Africa Association (EAA) grouping British companies in the region, hailed Cheserem's commitment to economic reforms.
He also gave rave reviews to Cheserem's commitment to continued liberalisation to spur growth of the economy.
In the aftermath of July 7 violence, in which at least nine people were killed, Cheserem emerged as a key leader urging the government to seek dialogue to end the political stalemate.
"The actions of July 7 will not be repeated. We are moving fast. We want a stable country fit for all to invest and live in peacefully," Cheserem told a media reception on Wednesday.
"In future, it is likely that police will walk behind demonstrators to protect them rather than harass them. That is the way to go," Cheserem added.

Opposition leaders accused the government of printing cash before 1992 elections to help finance Moi's win. The result was spiralling inflation and annual interest rates of up to 85 percent and the shilling falling in value.

A career accountant, the governor was commercial director of Lever Brothers Malawi Ltd and other Unilever Group subsidiaries in Malawi when he was called to replace Eric Kotut, under whose reign financial abuse was rampant and bad management thrived.
Vimal Shah, managing director at leading palm oil dealers Bidco Oil Refineries Ltd, called the governor's re-appointment "positive and encouraging, a step in the forward mode".
"His mandate for another four years will help reassure the business community in a volatile political period," said John Munge, managing director at brokerage Shah, Munge & Partners.
